topic: Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)
subject: physics

items.q: In physics, what does the word 'fluid' mean?
items.correct: A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas.
items.misconception: A fluid must be a liquid, never a gas.
items.why: In everyday English 'fluid' is used to mean a runny liquid, and the word appears on drink bottles and in medicine, never in connection with gases. In physics a fluid is anything that can flow. Gases flow, so a fluid can be either a liquid or a gas.
items.random_wrong: A fluid is anything that can be poured.

items.q: A gas is sealed inside a container. In which direction does the pressure of the gas exert a force on the container walls?
items.correct: At right angles to each wall surface.
items.misconception: Downwards on every part of the container.
items.why: Students learn that pressure at depth comes from the weight of liquid above, and weight acts downwards, so they carry that single direction over to the force on every surface. The weight explains how big the pressure is, not which way the force acts. At any point the pressure pushes at right angles to whatever surface is there — sideways on a wall, upwards on the underside of a submerged object.
items.random_wrong: Sideways along each wall surface.

items.q: A crate rests on the floor. It exerts a force of 300 N normal to the floor over a contact area of 0.25 m². What pressure does the crate exert on the floor?
items.misconception: 75 Pa
items.why: 'More area' sounds like 'more of everything', and students multiply the two given numbers rather than reading the equation as a division. Read p = F/A as 'force shared out over the area'. Spreading the same force over more area gives each square metre less force, so the pressure falls — which is why snowshoes stop you sinking.

items.q: A pressure of 400 Pa acts normal to a surface of area 0.20 m². What is the size of the force acting normal to that surface?
items.why: Students remember the shape of the equation, p = F/A, rather than rearranging it, and dividing the larger number by the smaller feels safe. Rearrange properly. From p = F/A, F = p A and A = F/p. Only the pressure is found by dividing.
items.random_wrong: 80 Pa

items.q: Which units must be used in p = F/A so that the pressure comes out in pascals?
items.correct: F in newtons and A in metres squared
items.misconception: F in newtons and A in centimetres squared
items.why: The equation makes no mention of units, and dividing the two numbers as printed gives a tidy-looking answer. For an answer in pascals, F must be in newtons and A in metres squared. Convert the area first, every time.
items.random_wrong: F in kilograms and A in metres squared

items.q: A drawing pin is pushed into a board. The force on its flat head and the force at its sharp point are the same size. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The pressure at the point is greater, because the area there is smaller.
items.misconception: The pressure at the point is smaller, because the contact area is smaller.
items.why: 'More area' sounds like 'more of everything', and students multiply the two given numbers rather than reading the equation as a division. Read p = F/A as 'force shared out over the area'. Spreading the same force over more area gives each square metre less force, so the pressure falls — which is why snowshoes stop you sinking.
items.random_wrong: The pressure is the same at both, because the same force acts at both ends.

items.q: A force of 60 N acts normal to a surface of area 20 cm². What is the pressure on that surface?
items.misconception: 3 Pa
items.why: The equation makes no mention of units, and dividing the two numbers as printed gives a tidy-looking answer. For an answer in pascals, F must be in newtons and A in metres squared. Convert the area first, every time.
items.random_wrong: 300 Pa

items.q: Which statement best describes the Earth's atmosphere?
items.correct: A thin layer of air that gets less dense with height.
items.misconception: A thick layer of air with the same density at all heights.
items.why: Air is invisible and feels identical from day to day, so students have no everyday evidence that it thins out with height. Air is squashed by the weight of the air above it, so it is most dense near the ground and becomes steadily less dense with increasing altitude.
items.random_wrong: A thin layer of air that gets more dense with altitude.

items.q: Why does atmospheric pressure decrease as the height above the ground increases?
items.correct: There is less air above the surface, so less weight of air presses on it.
items.misconception: Gravity is much weaker high up, so the air presses on the surface less.
items.why: Students know gravity weakens with distance and know that astronauts float, so altitude is linked to 'less gravity' well before the numbers are considered. Over the height of a mountain the gravitational field strength is very nearly unchanged. What changes is the amount of air above you: as height increases there is always less air above a surface, so the pressure falls.
items.random_wrong: The air is colder high up, so its molecules press on surfaces less hard.

items.q: What creates atmospheric pressure on a surface?
items.correct: Air molecules colliding with the surface.
items.misconception: The wind blowing over the surface.
items.why: The only push from air a student actually feels is the wind, and weather forecasts talk about pressure and wind in the same breath. Air molecules are moving in all directions all the time, and their collisions press on every surface even in still air. Wind is a separate, extra effect.
items.random_wrong: Air molecules pushing each other sideways.

items.q: A weather balloon rises from ground level high into the atmosphere. What happens to the air outside the balloon as it rises?
items.correct: The density falls and the atmospheric pressure falls as well.
items.misconception: The density stays the same and the atmospheric pressure falls.
items.why: Air is invisible and feels identical from day to day, so students have no everyday evidence that it thins out with height. Air is squashed by the weight of the air above it, so it is most dense near the ground and becomes steadily less dense with increasing altitude.
items.random_wrong: The density falls but the atmospheric pressure stays the same.

items.q: A diver is 12 m below the surface of water of density 1000 kg/m³. In this question use g = 9.8 N/kg. What is the pressure due to the water at that depth?
items.why: Two of the three numbers appear in the question wording as the obvious data, and g is quoted separately, so it is easily left out of the substitution. Write the equation out and substitute all three quantities in order. Leaving g out makes the answer about ten times too small.

items.q: Which set of units must be used in p = h ρ g to give the pressure in pascals?
items.correct: h in m, ρ in kg/m³, g in N/kg
items.misconception: h in m, ρ in g/cm³, g in N/kg
items.why: g/cm³ is the unit used in density practicals, so it is the form students remember, and the equation itself does not display units. Convert first: multiply a density in g/cm³ by 1000 to get kg/m³. Using 1 instead of 1000 makes the answer a thousand times too small.
items.random_wrong: h in m, ρ in kg/m³, g in N

items.q: A tank contains oil of density 900 kg/m³ to a depth of 2.5 m. In this question use g = 9.8 N/kg. What is the pressure due to the oil at the base of the tank?
items.why: Two of the three numbers appear in the question wording as the obvious data, and g is quoted separately, so it is easily left out of the substitution. Write the equation out and substitute all three quantities in order. Leaving g out makes the answer about ten times too small.

items.q: Why is the pressure at a point in a liquid greater when there is a taller column of liquid above that point?
items.correct: There is a greater weight of liquid pressing down on that point.
items.misconception: The liquid at the bottom is squashed into a smaller space.
items.why: Students transfer the gas model, where compressing a gas does raise its pressure, to a liquid, and picture the lower water being crushed. Liquids are very hard to compress, and their density is treated as constant. The pressure rises with depth because of the weight of the column above, which is exactly what p = h ρ g says.
items.random_wrong: Deeper liquid always has a greater density than shallow liquid.

items.q: A diver swims from a depth of 4.0 m to a depth of 10.0 m in water of density 1000 kg/m³. In this question use g = 9.8 N/kg. By how much does the pressure due to the water increase?
items.why: Every earlier question has asked for the pressure at a depth, so students apply the same routine and substitute the one depth they can see. Read the question: a difference in pressure needs a difference in height. Subtract the two depths first, then multiply by ρ and g.

items.q: Why does a totally submerged object experience an upthrust?
items.correct: The pressure on its bottom surface is greater than on its top surface.
items.misconception: The liquid underneath pushes up on it and nothing pushes down on it.
items.why: Students notice the upward push they feel in a swimming pool and do not think about the water sitting on top of a submerged object also pushing down. Both surfaces are pushed. The bottom face is deeper, so the pressure and the force there are bigger. Upthrust is the difference between the two, not the bottom force alone.
items.random_wrong: Liquid pressure acts upwards only, so anything in a liquid is pushed up.

items.q: A solid object is placed in a liquid. Under what condition does the object float?
items.correct: When the object's density is less than the liquid's density.
items.misconception: When the object is light, whatever the liquid it is placed in.
items.why: Most everyday floating objects a student handles are small and light, and most sinking ones are dense metals or stones, so weight and density are never separated. Compare densities, not weights. A steel ship weighs thousands of tonnes and floats; a steel nail weighs a few grams and sinks. What matters is the density of the object compared with the density of the liquid.
items.random_wrong: When the upthrust on the object is greater than its weight.

items.q: The pressure due to a column of water is 4900 Pa. The water has a density of 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg. What is the height of the column?
items.why: Two of the three numbers appear in the question wording as the obvious data, and g is quoted separately, so it is easily left out of the substitution. Write the equation out and substitute all three quantities in order. Leaving g out makes the answer about ten times too small.

items.q: Two open tanks are filled with water to the same depth. Tank Y is four times as wide as tank X. How does the pressure due to the water at the base of the tanks compare?
items.correct: The same in both, because the water is at the same depth in each.
items.misconception: Greater in tank Y, because tank Y contains four times as much water.
items.why: Students reason from total weight rather than from weight per unit area; a bigger tank obviously contains a heavier load of water. The extra weight in a wide tank is spread over a proportionally wider base, so the pressure is unchanged. Only h, ρ and g appear in the equation.
items.random_wrong: Greater in tank X, because the base of tank X has a much smaller area.

items.q: A cube is held completely under water. Its top face is 0.10 m below the surface and its bottom face is 0.30 m below. The water has a density of 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.8 N/kg. What is the difference in pressure between the bottom face and the top face?
items.why: Every earlier question has asked for the pressure at a depth, so students apply the same routine and substitute the one depth they can see. Read the question: a difference in pressure needs a difference in height. Subtract the two depths first, then multiply by ρ and g.
items.random_wrong: 980 Pa

items.q: A solid block of density 700 kg/m³ is lowered into water of density 1000 kg/m³ and released. What happens to the block?
items.correct: It floats with part of it below the surface of the water.
items.misconception: It floats with all of it above the surface of the water.
items.why: The phrase 'floats on water' suggests resting on top, and students see the exposed part of a boat far more clearly than the hull beneath. The object must be partially submerged, or there would be no surfaces at different depths and so no upthrust to hold it up.
items.random_wrong: It sinks, because a solid block is heavier than water.

items.q: Water flows along a pipe. Which way does the water pressure push on the pipe wall?
items.correct: At right angles to the pipe wall, outwards. Pressure causes a force normal to the surface, not a force along it.
items.misconception: The pressure pushes along the surface, in the direction the fluid is moving.
items.why: Students merge the idea of pressure with the idea of flow, so the push is imagined to point wherever the fluid is going. Separate the two ideas. Flow is the movement of the fluid; pressure produces a force normal (at right angles) to any surface the fluid touches, whatever direction the fluid is moving.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A force of 300 N acts normal to an area of 0.25 m². Is the answer 1200 N or 1200 Pa?
items.correct: 1200 Pa. Pressure and force are different quantities: force is measured in newtons, N, and pressure in pascals, Pa.
items.misconception: Pressure is just another word for the force pushing on something, so the answer can be given in newtons.
items.why: Everyday speech uses 'pressure' and 'force' interchangeably ('press harder'), and both are about pushing. Force is the push itself, in newtons. Pressure is the force on each square metre, in pascals. A 1200 Pa answer written as 1200 N loses the mark even though the arithmetic is right.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A block of mass 5 kg presses on a surface. Can you use 5 as the value of F in p = F/A?
items.correct: No. F must be a force in newtons. The mass in kilograms must first be turned into a weight in newtons using weight = mass × gravitational field strength.
items.misconception: The 'force' in the pressure equation is the mass of the object, because that is what is pushing down.
items.why: In everyday use 'how heavy something is' is quoted in kilograms, so kilograms feel like the natural measure of a push. Check the unit of every quantity before substituting: F is in newtons, N. Kilograms measure mass, not force.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At the same depth, is the pressure the same in water and in mercury?
items.correct: No. Pressure due to a column of liquid depends on the density of the liquid as well as the height, so the denser liquid gives the greater pressure at the same depth.
items.misconception: Only the depth matters; the liquid it is made of makes no difference.
items.why: Depth is the variable used in every classroom example, and density is an unfamiliar quantity that students do not picture as 'weight of each cubic metre'. Density is a factor in p = h ρ g. A denser liquid has more mass, and so more weight, in the same column, so it produces a greater pressure at the same depth.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A block is floating at rest on water. How does the upthrust compare with its weight?
items.correct: They are equal. The block is at rest, so the resultant force on it is zero and the upthrust balances the weight.
items.misconception: The upthrust must be bigger than the weight, otherwise the object would not stay up.
items.why: Students associate 'floating' with 'winning against gravity', and a bigger upward force feels like the reason the object is not sinking. A bigger upthrust would accelerate the object upwards out of the water. Because a floating object stays at rest, upthrust and weight must be equal in size.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How thick is the Earth's atmosphere compared with the Earth?
items.correct: It is a thin layer relative to the size of the Earth — a thin skin of air round a very large planet.
items.misconception: The atmosphere is a huge, deep blanket, far bigger than the Earth itself.
items.why: Space feels enormously far away, and diagrams of the atmosphere are usually drawn with the layers exaggerated so that they can be labelled. The specification is explicit: the atmosphere is a thin layer relative to the size of the Earth. Diagrams that show it as a deep shell are not drawn to scale.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Air is so light. How can it press on us at all?
items.correct: Air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure, and the column of air above any surface has a real weight — about 100 000 Pa of pressure at sea level.
items.misconception: Air weighs nothing, so atmospheric pressure must really be gravity acting directly on the surface.
items.why: A litre of air weighs almost nothing on a school balance, so students conclude air is weightless and look elsewhere for the cause of the pressure. Air does have mass and weight; there is simply a great deal of it above you. The pressure comes from the countless molecular collisions on the surface, and it decreases with height because less air is left above.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is g in p = h ρ g, and what unit does it have?
items.correct: g is the gravitational field strength, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. Its value is given in the question.
items.misconception: g is the weight of the object, measured in newtons.
items.why: g appears alongside weight in weight = mass × gravitational field strength, and both are labelled with newtons somewhere in the equation. Gravitational field strength is the force on each kilogram, so its unit is N/kg. It is a property of the place, not a force on an object.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How many square metres is 20 cm²?
items.correct: 0.0020 m². There are 10 000 cm² in 1 m², so divide by 10 000.
items.misconception: 1 cm = 0.01 m, so 1 cm² = 0.01 m² and 20 cm² = 0.20 m².
items.why: The length conversion is well known and is applied once, without squaring it, because the '²' is read as part of the unit's name rather than as an instruction. Squaring the length conversion squares the factor too: 1 m² = 100 cm × 100 cm = 10 000 cm². Dividing by 100 instead of 10 000 makes the pressure 100 times too small.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A question states g = 9.8 N/kg. Can you use 10 N/kg instead because it is easier?
items.correct: No. In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength will be given, and that is the value you must substitute.
items.misconception: g is always 10 N/kg — that is the number we always use.
items.why: Many early lessons round g to 10 N/kg to make the arithmetic easy, so the rounded value becomes the remembered one. Take g from the question every time. Using 10 instead of 9.8 shifts the answer by about 2%, which is enough to lose the accuracy mark.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the cold at high altitude explain the low atmospheric pressure there?
items.correct: No. Atmospheric pressure decreases with height because there are fewer air molecules, and so less weight of air, above the surface.
items.misconception: It is freezing up there, and cold air presses less hard, so the pressure is lower.
items.why: Students meet the gas relationship between temperature and pressure and reach for it because low temperature is the most obvious feature of high altitude. The explanation required here is the amount of air above the surface. As height increases there is always less air above than at a lower height, so the pressure falls.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Climbers carry oxygen at high altitude. Is that because oxygen causes atmospheric pressure?
items.correct: No. All the air molecules colliding with a surface create atmospheric pressure, not the oxygen alone; the atmosphere is mostly nitrogen.
items.misconception: There is less oxygen high up, and oxygen is what makes the pressure, so the pressure is lower.
items.why: 'Thin air' is discussed in biology lessons and in the news in terms of oxygen for breathing, so oxygen becomes the whole story about altitude. Every air molecule that collides with a surface contributes to the pressure. There is less of all of it high up, because there is less air above that height.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A block has a density of 700 kg/m³. Will it float?
items.correct: In water, of density 1000 kg/m³, yes — but you must compare the two densities. The same block would sink in a liquid of density 600 kg/m³.
items.misconception: You can tell whether something floats from its own density on its own.
items.why: Water is used in nearly every example, so its density becomes an invisible standard and students learn a rule of thumb such as 'floats if less than 1000'. Always compare the object's density with the density of the liquid it is in. Floating depends on the pair of densities, not on one number.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How do you find the difference in pressure between a depth of 0.10 m and a depth of 0.30 m?
items.correct: Use the difference in height, 0.20 m: difference in pressure = 0.20 × ρ × g.
items.misconception: You use both depths together, so you add them and use 0.40 m.
items.why: Students know that both numbers must be used somewhere, and adding is the operation they reach for when combining two values. A difference means a subtraction. Take the shallower depth away from the deeper one, then multiply by ρ and g.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an object weigh less when it is under water?
items.correct: No. Its weight is unchanged; the upthrust is an extra upward force, so the resultant downward force — and the reading on a spring balance — is smaller.
items.misconception: Water makes objects lighter, so the object's weight becomes smaller in the liquid.
items.why: A stone really is easier to hold under water, and the balance reading really does drop, so 'lighter' is the natural description of what is observed. Weight = mass × gravitational field strength, and neither changes in water. What changes is the resultant force, because the upthrust now acts upwards as well.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Sand can be poured from a bucket. Is sand a fluid?
items.correct: No. A fluid can be either a liquid or a gas. Sand is a solid, even though grains of it can be poured.
items.misconception: Anything that can be poured is a fluid.
items.why: 'Can flow' is the usual one-line definition of a fluid, and pouring is how students test for flowing, so powders slip into the category. Use the specification's definition: a fluid is a liquid or a gas. Sand is a collection of solid grains sliding over one another.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.5.5 Pressure and pressure differences in fluids (physics only)
